utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness, now, mind that you don't mention your name or your profession, because otherwise your identity might be disclosed. But to begin with, tell us, at the time of the Serb aggression against Mostar, what happened to you or did anything important happen to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, important. What important happened? During the Serb aggression, I was captured by Serb troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Will you tell us when was that and how did it come about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, my mother lived in Rodoc, and I went there to bring her to my place, and I was caught by the Serb army at Cekrk. They seized my car, and I don't know, something else. And I remained there surrounded. They wouldn't let me come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could you tell us when was that, what month? And how long did you remain surrounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I was there on the -- from the 11th of May until the 11th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And tell us, how did you get out of that, those surroundings? How did you manage to free yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: On the 11th of June, the HVO troops arrived. They got through Cekrk and that's how I got free. That's how I was made free on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So the Serbs withdrew and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: After that, were you engaged in the military in some way? During the Serb aggression were you militarily engaged somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: About the 15th of June, I registered with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could you tell us which unit that was and what duties you had within that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: That was a PZO, anti-aircraft defence unit, and my duty, I manned a Bofors 40 millimetre gun. My duties involved observation, monitoring planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell us, how long did you remain within HVO units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I was in the HVO units right up until the 9th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you left the HVO? How is it that you ceased to be an HVO soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I left the HVO quite simply. I quite simply didn't want to remain in the army any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that after the 9th of May, 1993, you stopped going to the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes. I stopped going there. I didn't want to go there any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What happened on that day, on the 9th of May, 1993? Could you describe that day? What was your experience on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, in the morning at about 5.15, shooting started. There was shooting from all directions. I looked out of the window in the direction of my combat post, and I saw that they were shooting from above. My combat post at Hum. And after perhaps, I don't know, maybe half an hour, some soldiers knocked on my door. I opened the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll stop you there and then we'll carry on. You say some soldiers were at your doors. Could you tell me, what soldiers were there? What sort of uniform did they have? What sort of insignia did they have? Did you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms. They had HVO insignia on them, and they had red ribbons around their arms, red, white, and blue. I couldn't recognise anyone because their dialect wasn't the Mostar dialect either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened then? They turned up at the door. What do they want? What did they do? What did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: They wanted me to show them my identity card. I did that. I showed them my HVO identity card. They had a looked around the flat. It was not very serious. They saw my weapon there. They saw my rifle there. They returned my identity card and they quite simply left. They visited other parts of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me, the rifle that they saw, did they confiscate it or did they leave it there? Was that a rifle that you had from the HVO unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes. That was my rifle. I had been issued with that rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did they take it with them or did they leave it there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: They left it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And then what did the soldiers do in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: They visited the entire building. They visited all the flats in the building. They took the Muslims out of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: How many people did they take out and who did they take out? How many people did they take from all the families and how many families were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: There were four families there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And who did they take from those families?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: First of all, they took everyone away, all of them. No one remained in the flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Who were these people? Were they women, men, children? What age were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: There weren't any children, but there were husbands and wives with two grown-up sons, let's say. They were all older people. There were no children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And where did they take them and what happened to them on that day, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: They took them to the stadium. I couldn't see that, because I didn't leave my flat at the time, but I know that they went to the stadium. The women returned, and the men went to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did the women return on the same day, and did they return to their flats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes. They returned to their flats on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And in the meantime were their flats burgled or damaged in some way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You said that the other men from those four families were taken to the Heliodrom, as far as you know. Did they return to that building from the Heliodrom, and if they did, when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, they returned very quickly. I don't know. Maybe one month later, something like that. They returned to the building and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did they all return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And what then happened to them? Did they remain there? Did they go somewhere else? What happened to those neighbours of yours then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, I heard that they went to Croatia, to some camp, and that they then left that camp and went to Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And tell me, did they -- did each person go individually or did they go there in some organised way? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I think that it was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You mean when they left Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: It was organised. I was told that there were buses there near the stadium, and at the Heliodrom they said who would remain there and who would be leaving Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And these neighbours of yours, did they ever return to their flats from Norway? Did you ever see them again after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes. They returned and they are in Mostar now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do all those who lived in that building in May 1993, did they all return to the flats in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me, on the 9th of May, 1993, apart from the HVO soldiers you saw, were any -- did any other soldiers go to your flat on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: At about 9.00, they knocked on my door again. I opened the door. I saw men wearing camouflage uniforms again. They had insignia on their arms. They had the BH Army lily sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Due mean 9.00 in the morning or 9.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: This was at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there, and how do you know that they were members of the BH Army? Did they introduce themselves as such or did you recognise them by their insignia? What did they want?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: They didn't introduce themselves. They asked me to show them my identity card, which I did. They took me outside, out of the flat. They asked me if there were any men in the building, and I said that there weren't any men there. They told me to stand in a corner, in case someone fired at them from the building. They said that if that happened, they would kill me first of all. I told them that there was no there to fire at them. All the men who remained in the building were old people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: When they asked you to show them your identity card, you didn't so them your HVO identity card?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I didn't show them my HVO identity card. I couldn't show them that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Which one did you show them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I showed them my old identity card.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Your personal identity card. Very well. And tell me, that rifle that remained there, what happened to it? Did they carry out a search? What happened to the rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: No, they didn't search the flat. And I put -- I'd hidden the rifle because I thought anyone might turn up at that time. I'd hidden the rifle behind a cupboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And how long did those BH army soldiers remain there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: They spent maybe about ten minutes there, until shooting broke out from a garden across the road from my building. And then the windows in the building started -- were shattered, and they left the building and I remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Let's just finish with the subject of the rifle. Did you have that rifle throughout the wartime period or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: No. As soon as the shooting had subsided a bit, maybe on the third or fourth day, as soon as the situation had calmed down, my unit was at the university, and at that point everything that I had been issued with, I returned all these thing to the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So you returned your weapon then. You returned the equipment that you had, the equipment and weapon you'd been given in your unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me, apart from those two incidents on the 9th of May, were any other attempts made? Did anyone else turn up at your door, some groups of men, and were you bothered, disturbed in some way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: No. On the 9th of May, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And after that, in the following days, did anything happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Later on, yes. Perhaps there were individual incidents. Someone would turn up. But I wasn't really disturbed by anyone. But they would just count the people in the flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know who those soldiers were? Were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes, they were soldiers, but I didn't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, at that time did you know Vinko Martinovic, Stela? And if you did, how well did you know him and where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, up until the war, I knew Vinko Martinovic, Stela, only by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you know his family at the time? Did you know a member of his family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I knew his father, Ivan, and his brother Jadranko, because I had -- I worked with his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. On the map you showed us, that that base was not far from your building, the base Vinko Martinovic, Stela, was. During that time, did you go to Vinko Martinovic's base? Did you ever meet him there yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: For how long -- how often did you go to that base during that period up until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, I went to the base -- I'd go there if I felt that something Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French English transcripts in the building -- if I felt that something would happen, if I felt that someone might disturb us or drive us out. I would then go there and turn to Stela for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So tell us, how would you turn to him for help? How would you be welcomed? What would you say? What would he say? And what would you ask him for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: He always gave me a warm welcome. And I would tell him, for example, that some people had turned up. Someone would come during the day to look through the building, and then would try and drive you out during the evening. And I would tell Stela that somebody turned up and he would say it was no problem because his unit was not far away. He said that there were would be no problems and no one would bother us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did he give you the possibility of calling him or informing him? Did he promise he would show up, something to at that effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said, "If you need anything, tell us and we'll -- we'll go there immediately."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You said you went to see Stela for those reasons. Did you go to that base for any other reasons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I went there because my mother was in Rodoc and at that time it was only possible to go there through Varda, because you couldn't use the main road to go to Rodoc. So I would have to go down there to visit my mother in Rodoc, and I would go in Stela's van, the van from the base, which went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could you tell us why that van from the base went, when, and why was it convenient for you to go with that van? Could we try to explain this to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, the van went in the morning at about 7.00. And it was convenient for me to go in that van because my mother was near the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And where did the van go, to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes, to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And tell me, Rodoc, where your mother lived, how far was that from the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: The Heliodrom is in Rodoc itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. And you said that you would go in that van. Did Stela know about that? Did you ask him for that? Did he give you permission for this? And how did this take place? You would leave at 7.00 in the morning. When would you return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes. Stela allowed me to go with that van, and I would leave in the morning at 7.00, and then I would spend the following day in Rodoc, and the next day in the morning when the van went to pick up the detainees, I would get in and return to Mostar again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And how often did you use this service? How much did you go there in this van?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, at least once a week, because I thought it was necessary. I had to take some things there for my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. And how often did you go to Stela's unit? How often did you go to that unit? How many times a month or a week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, maybe twice a week because I was bored, since at the time there was nothing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And when you went to Stela's unit, what would you do there? What were your reasons for go there? How did you spend your time is there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, I never did anything over there. We'd sit, have coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Who did you sit with? Was it with Stela? Did you sit with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, mostly with Stela.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me, when you went to the base, did you see any prisoners of war there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know where these prisoners of war were from? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: From the Heliodrom, because this van that I used would bring them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you know any of them personally? Did you know those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could you tell us, did you talk to them? Did they tell you what it was like at Stela's? Did they complain? Did they say what it was like in that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes, I did speak with them. On the whole, they didn't complain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. And did you personally see the conditions in which they were living? Did you see what sort of work they had to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: As far as work is concerned, well, maybe it had to do with construction, cleaning up, putting the base into order, repairs, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Were these people under guard? Were they supervised? What sort of control was there over them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: There was no guard. No type of -- no kind of supervision either. It wasn't necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there in the base around those prisoners? How many soldiers would usually deal with those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You'd go to that base. You'd see the prisoners. And how many soldiers in the base itself were controlling those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: There were never very many prisoners there during the day because the soldiers were mostly at the front. There were very few soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. So you said these prisoners would work in the base. Were they working in dangerous conditions? Was there any shooting? What was the security situation like? Was that an area that was dangerous or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: It was the safe area because it was very far from the front line. So there weren't any problems. There was no danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you see whether those prisoners were able to receive visits? Did anyone go to visit them in were you ever able to see this happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes. Family members came to visit them. They'd bring them clothes, food, and similar things that they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you see any of them going home? Was anyone allowed to go home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Some people went home for an hour or two hours, have a bath, a change of clothes, and would then return. No one escorted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you see anyone maltreating prisoners or beating prisoners? Did you notice any bruises on these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: No. I never saw anything like that on the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of the detainees was killed there or wounded while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: No. I don't know about anyone being killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you ever see any detainees going to work in the vicinity of the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: No. I never saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And tell me, did you ever go down to the medical centre yourself, where the demarcation line was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: No. I never went down to the line. I wasn't a soldier, so no, I couldn't approach the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me, did you ever see Stela and his soldiers going to drive Muslims out of the their flats or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: No. I never saw something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you ever hear people speaking about that? Did you ever hear anyone saying that Stela and his soldiers expelled people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: After the war there were rumours in the town, but I personally never saw something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you ever check up on any of those stories? Did you ever try to verify whether it was true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I knew some people -- sometimes I asked some people, some people I was sure of, some people for whom I know that they didn't know Stela. Let's say they say, "Stela drove me out," and then I would ask them to provide me with a description. I said, "Describe Stela to me." And they would give me a totally false description. It had nothing to do with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: How would he be described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, the last time a woman described him to me, she said he was big, wore an earring, had a ponytail, was tall. He never was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you see how Stela treated the Muslims at the time? Did they go to his unit to ask him for something or were they afraid of going there? What was his attitude towards Muslims, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, his attitude, I don't know. Quite a few Muslims went to the base to ask Stela to make it possible for them to leave the town, to go to Croatia, to other countries, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And tell me, was Stela able to do anything for them? Was it possible for him to help these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I don't think that Stela could have done it, because I think that he could have told them whom to contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: When these people went to the base were you afraid of him? Were they afraid of his action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: No, they weren't afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me. You said you knew other members of Stela's family. You said you knew his father, brother, et cetera. Do you know how they treated the Muslims in the neighbourhood at the time, what their relationship to the Muslims was? For example, his father, his family.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I know that there were up to seven or eight Muslims in his house. For example, if something happened, he didn't try to conceal who was in his house. Stela knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness, I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded my examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, is it your testimony that actually you did not know Stela before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I didn't, no. Not personally. I knew him just like that, by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And why did you go to him for help if you did not know him well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I did it because I was on good terms with his brother. And Stela knew that Jadranko and I were fine, so it was not difficult for me to go to him, to turn to him, because he knew that with his brother, I was like a brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what kind of help could he render to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: The kind of help? Well, the most important kind of help for me was that I be left alone to have -- to keep my house. That was the most important kind of help.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who was disturbing you in your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Who? Who disturbed me? I think -- well, it's difficult to say now. All sorts of troops went by so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did any soldiers apart from those soldiers from some Muslim unit, did any other soldiers visit you at home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: It was your testimony that on one occasion some Muslim soldiers visited you at home, and my question was: Did any other soldiers visit you after that, after the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, yes. Individuals did come to the building severally. I don't know. For instance, I don't know when the darkness fell perhaps those would come back to harass us or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you mean individuals in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: In military uniforms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: To which units did they belong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Which units? It's impossible to guess. I mean, in Mostar there were units from all over, from Central Bosnia to -- I don't know, to what.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Where they Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, mostly those who came usually had HVO patches.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What were their requests to the people living in your building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, nothing special. They didn't have any particular requests. What we were afraid most of at that time was, say, looters, plunderers, because those were the times. Anybody could come by night and rob you. From nothing special. There was nothing special for them to look for.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did they loot your house, your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know what position did Stela occupy at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What position did they occupy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: You mean like commander of the unit or front lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: First of all, I ask you was he a military person or not? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French English transcripts

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Stela was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was he wearing any military uniform with patches, badges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: He wore a camouflage uniform, but I never saw any patches.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know what military rank did he have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I am not aware of any rank of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was he commander of any military formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Why, he was the commander. There was a base there on Kalemova Street, and he was a commander. He had some 30, 40 men, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of unit was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: The kind of unit on Bulevar down there. They had a section of the front line they manned. But some speciality of theirs, well, I wouldn't know. What was there? Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what kind of functions did his unit perform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: What kind of function? As far as I know, their chief task was to guard that line, there on the Bulevar. Something else, some task at that time, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know who was Stela's immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Direct, immediate? I don't think they had anyone above.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was it a regular unit or any unit without any command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, all those units were not under anyone. I mean, under any command. I don't know that any -- that anyone had some superior command, any command above them, any of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, is it your testimony that you visited Stela's unit, Stela's base, on very, very rare occasions, somewhere around two weeks or two times a week? Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes, I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I asked you was it on very rare occasions that you visited Stela's base.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Seldom. I don't know what you mean, rare visits. I said I would visit about twice a week. Now, what do you mean by "rare occasion?"

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So you did not go there every day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: No. No. There was no need for me to go there every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So you -- you did not know what was happening on the base every day, on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, of course I didn't know what happened there on a daily basis because I wasn't there every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know any of the prisoners who were taken to Stela's base from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, we should move into a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: My question was: Did you see them on very many occasions, many times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, I saw them there several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of job did they perform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, jobs. Mostly cleaning around, sweeping the base, some construction work, repairing cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Sorry. Did you enter Stela's base? I mean the building itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I didn't enter the building. I was in the yard, in the yard of the building. I didn't go into the building because there was no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Is it correct that some prisoners were staying there overnight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I am not aware of anyone staying there overnight. Nobody stayed overnight, I'm quite sure. Not in the base. Or at least as far as I know. I'm quite sure that nobody did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know any of Stela's soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Why, yes, I did know some, because they were Mostarans. They were mostly from the town, so I -- but they were all younger than I. They were all younger. At least 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know Ernest Takac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I knew Ernest by sight only.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What was his position within the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, let me see. He was just a foot soldier. I think just a foot soldier. I don't know that he had anything special.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have -- did you happen to work with other prisoners at Stela's base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Who me? No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And how many prisoners, just approximately, they would bring to his -- to his base? To Stela's base, I mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, about -- it would be a smaller van with about ten seats or so, but there would be more people in it. So it would be about 15, 20 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And do you know if any of them were in other places than the base itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I don't know that they worked at other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know how Vinko Martinovic introduced himself to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Introduced himself. No, I don't know. Everybody called him Stela. What else? I don't know how else he would introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And prisoners called him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Stela.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, is it your testimony that you knew Jadranko Martinovic well; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And you also stated that at some point you worked with him. When and where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: With Jadranko. I worked with him. Jadranko worked for Slavonija Di before the war. He's an architect and all the jobs that he did, he invited me to do the tiling, and we used to do it for years before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: For how much years did you work together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: We worked together. For not less than six or seven years before the war. Perhaps more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And did you maintain a relationship with him during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: We continued to be on good terms, of course, but Jadranko, during the war, was not in Mostar during the war. He worked else where for Eurohertz.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that some people from Heliodrom were at some point taken to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: They were not -- I mean, not taken. I think that at the Heliodrom they had to state where they wanted to go. So some stayed in Mostar, and some said they wanted to go to third countries. So some stayed in Mostar, and some left for third countries. Those were the times. I mean, people said where they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You just stated that some people from your neighbourhood were taken to Heliodrom and some went to some Scandinavian country; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And some -- for some time they were kept in some refugee camp, right, in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Yes, for a while they were in some refugee camps. I don't know which camp in Croatia, exactly, but they were there until, I suppose, those other countries said they would admit them, until they had it all arranged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How many years did your neighbours or people whom you knew stayed abroad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, I think until 1997, 1998, and then everybody came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, is it your testimony that after the war you heard some rumours about some unlawful actions committed by Stela's soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: After the war, after the war, yes, there was talk, but these stories, you can never stop them. I don't know how to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did the people tell you about some particular incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Very rarely. Very seldom somebody would say something specific, but, for instance, I heard these cases when somebody talked. But those were people who talked immediately after the war when you just crossed from one side to the other, say, and then somebody says -- there were, for instance, such cases how they said they had been driven away by Stela but he never knew Stela. But there were, you know, such -- there were several of those armies, you know. For instance, people would write on the wall where somebody has been chased away, and it says, for instance, "Stela," yet inside you have somebody completely different. So there were such cases when Stela had absolutely nothing to do, couldn't have anything to do with some cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How do you know that, that he had nothing to do with it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, say, how can I not know. He had nothing to do with it. If on the doors, for instance, you have "Stela" written on the door and inside you find somebody from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you hear also rumours about Stela's soldiers committing any unlawful acts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: How shall I put it? Those were all rumours. It was all the grapevine. They were those tales which were spun of all sorts. I mean, I don't trust all these tales, because at that time people did all sorts of things in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Why did you try to ask people to describe Stela? What was your problem with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really care all that much, but when I did that, I didn't have a clue that I'd be coming here as a witness. It was a long time ago. What was important? It was important because I knew him. And I realised that somebody didn't know Stela, that he didn't have an idea who was Stela, that he was saying no matter what. I never thought that I'd be coming here. I mean, at the time when I was after it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know to whom the base, I mean the building where Stela's base was located, belonged to before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did it belong to Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Before the war, no. I don't know. I don't know if it belonged to Stela before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, were any of your next of kin, let's say close relatives and maybe people whom you knew well, arrested in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: In 1993. Only, say, my brother-in-law. He was arrested. But I mean no. I don't have any other relatives, I mean any other close relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: By whom was he arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I haven't the slightest. He was taken away from his flat to the Heliodrom at around 2.00 in the morning. But he used to live in a completely different part of the town where -- where I don't think Stela had any influence, because, for instance, I'm in one part of the town, and he's in a completely different part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know which part of the city was Stela in command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: I don't know which part of the town he had under his command but I assume, I guess, because his base was near the Rondo, then, say, that it was probably there, because there were several of those bases in Mostar, more than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How long did your relative stay in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MK
utterances.text: Well, six months, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all. My cross-examination is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think we'll break here. We will resume at quarter to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have no other questions, Your Honours. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French English transcripts

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now, Witness, thank you very much for coming here to give your evidence. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the witness is leaving, Your Honour, thank you for letting me take the floor. I would like to say that we will be requiring the same protective measures for the next witness aside from voice distortion. So this special microphone won't be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So at this stage, do you have any documents to tender? Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. This is the map, D2/36 --/35. I apologise. D2/35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So this document D2/35 is admitted under seal. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I was waiting for my turn. I didn't want to make any comments up until now. Just for the sake of the transcript, I wanted to say with regard to the Prosecutor's allegation that the document that they used, 601.1, which is allegedly a book - I don't know what he called it - from the Heliodrom, we don't have evidence of any kind to this effect. We have no evidence showing that it's a list of any kind from the Heliodrom. It could be from anywhere. And for the record, I would like to say that the Defence objects to such allegations on the part of the Prosecution. The Prosecution can't say where this document comes from and what it represents. This is only something that they can assume. This is not a claim that they can make. This is not an entire document, and apart from a few names and a few dates, it doesn't state anything else, and the names of individual units. What it actually represents, we don't know. And I just wanted to say this for the sake of the record. And my colleague has told me that the document is 567.1. The classification number I mentioned was the wrong one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe this document has been admitted into evidence. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about the next document, 601.1? Well, the next document is 601.1 has not been used at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It hasn't been used today but last time we made a written objection, Your Honours, and I think you have already received our objection regarding this document. But today this document was not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, we checked. It was admitted on the 18th of July. I mean the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mean the document 601.1?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since this document has not been used, at this time we will not discuss about it. We'll check whether it has been admitted or not. Could we have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you will be shown a piece of paper bearing your first and last names. Don't read it out aloud. If it is correct, if the name is yours, just say yes. Just say yes if it's correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: If the first and last names are correct, just say yes. Don't read it out. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your pseudonym will be ML, but I will just address you as "Witness." That will makes things easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness, as far as you can remember, when the Serbian aggressor of the JNA attacked Mostar, what happened to you? Were you engaged in the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: During the war against the Serbs, I wasn't in the army. I was commander of the Civil Defence in our local commune, in our neighbourhood, that is to say. And at the same time, I helped my wife a bit with the food, because the army would go and eat in our restaurant too at the time. I'd just like to clarify this post in the Civil Defence. We were ordered to deliver food, the humanitarian aid that at the time got delivered to Mostar. We had to clean up public shelters because the companies for cleaning up weren't functioning at the time. We cleaned up the surrounding buildings and did other small jobs of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When we mention -- when we talk about your restaurant, don't name it, so as to prevent your identity from being revealed. Did your restaurant continue to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Yes, it did. The restaurant worked throughout the period, but it was used for the needs of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you remember the 9th of May, 1993, when the conflict broke out between the BH Army and the HVO in Mostar? What happened to you at the time? Where were you and what did you personally see and hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Since the shooting had already stopped for a period of time, on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French English transcripts the 9th of May, in the early morning hours, loud explosions could be heard, shooting. And since my house is within rifle range, rifles from the Bulevar, I heard shooting. Only my wife and myself were in the house. The children were with their grandparents in a village. I got up to see what was happening. I saw young men in uniforms in the street. They were running from the direction of Balinovac. That became a base only later. They were running towards the secondary school building, that is to say, towards the Bulevar. At that point in time, nobody had the time to ask anyone else what was happening when they were running. Only three or four hours later, when someone returned from down there because new people would turn up, some people were going and some people were returning from there, it was then that I learned that the line of demarcation, from the Savici Street [phoen] location, that I learned that an attack had been launched from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: On that day or in that morning, that morning, did you see Vinko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw Vinko Martinovic and about another ten young men from the neighbourhood, from Balinovac. They ran down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: On that day did you notice that something was happening in your neighbourhood? Did you see anything happening to your Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: At that moment, there was no one in the street. What happened to these people in their homes, I don't know. I have three houses in the neighbourhood in which Muslims live, and at the time, they didn't go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: But otherwise did you have -- were you aware of the fact that they were being taken away somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: There were rumours but I personally didn't go because civilians were not allowed to move very freely around the town. I was told that they were being taken away to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you see or hear them returning to their flats later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: For a certain period of time, as far as I can remember, Mr. Armin Pohar established the Muslim democratic league. I think that's what it's called. The Muslim Democratic Party. And they would visit people in the Heliodrom, and anyone who wanted to join the party could do so and return home. They could go to the left bank - let's call it like that - or they could go to other countries through some humanitarian organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How do you know all of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Well, I know this because the army assembled there and there were rumours. People would talk, and we have a radio there, television. It's not such a backwoods after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: After the 9th of May, 1993, what did you do? Did your restaurant continue to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Yes it did. We continued to work. My wife continued to work there, and the stocks that remained were left for our friends, who later on when they gathered in the unit, because most of their wives and their children went there, so my wife would do washing for them until all that had been organised and until we started receiving regular provisions from the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When did you see Vinko Martinovic and his soldiers entering the building that you have pointed out on the map in Kalemova? When was the unit formed? When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: The unit was formed maybe seven or ten days after the 9th of May. And maybe after my recommendation, too, because in my neighbourhood I saw that empty house. It belonged to an officer, a former JNA officer, Panto Skoro. He was a Colonel. That was his rank. And before the conflict with the Serbs broke out, he left the house. Half of it was his, and the other half belonged to the Kajtas family. He was retired. He received a pension from Slovenia because he was a commercial salesman. He left that house with his children and he went to Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When did that family leave the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: In the course of the war with the Serbs, maybe two or three months later. Then somebody had a nervous breakdown. She had a nervous breakdown, so they left the house and it was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How long did that house remain empty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: For five months for sure. From the time when war broke out with the Serb. I can't remember when that was exactly. They were there for two or three months, and then they moved out, and it remained empty. So five or six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Was the building destroyed, damaged in some way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: The building was hit. The roof was hit. A projectile hit the roof, and one projectile hit a place between the garage and the house. So the house didn't have a roof, and the garage was half destroyed. There were no windows. The windowpanes had been broken. There was no electricity because the electricity installations had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know whether it was necessary to repair the house to make it possible for people to live in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It's impossible to sleep in a house if there are no windows. Quite a few repairs had to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You said that your restaurant continued working for the needs of the army. Could you describe how this functioned, what it looked like, how provision were is obtained, how you would provide meals.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: We would get beans, rice, et cetera, macaroni delivered by lorry, certain tins with half prepared food. There was some raw meat, chicken, sausages. We would prepare this. My wife prepared that because she was also a member of the unit. Every day we kept records of the amount of meals that were made to make sure that we weren't short of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you also keep records of the amount of meals that you prepared and gave out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Yes. We counted it according to the number of soldiers. So today, for example, I would consult Mr. Martinovic. On one day I'd consult him to see how many people there would be on the following day so we could work out how many meals would need to be prepared, more or less. So records were kept of this so we knew what we had received and what had been handed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know on this basis how many soldiers there were in the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: At the beginning, well, there were about 30 or 40 soldiers. And there were up to 70 soldiers. That was the maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you know the soldiers from the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: I knew quite a few soldiers, almost all of them, because after all, these were boys from our neighbourhood. Some from part of the avenue and some of them from the Rondo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How long have you known Vinko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Well, I knew him when he was a taxi driver. So that was about ten years before the war. We didn't have much contact, but we knew each other well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you provide Vinko Martinovic's units with food? Could you describe this for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Well, if raw food arrived from the warehouse, my wife would prepare it. They'd take a pot out and some plates. The soldiers would serve themselves. I'd collect the dishes after them once they had left because they all went there. They didn't -- food wasn't taken to them anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know what position that unit of Vinko Martinovic's had at the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Yes. They held the position next to the medical centre and the emergency department. They're next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were prisoners of a kind, who were in that base, who came and then stayed in that base on Kalemova Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Yes, I know about it. Prisoners, but I wouldn't call them prisoners. They were the ones who repaired the house and the garage, who built the roof, who again provided electricity. Well, there was prisoners, but they were together with them. They had a room where they slept. Some of them went to the Heliodrom to return the next morning. I wouldn't really call them prisoners. I would call them free prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many of them would there be there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: I do, because I provided meals for them. Between five and 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you meet them? Did you know them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Most of those prisoners, as I said, free prisoners, I knew from before the war because my -- I had -- they repaired my car. They repaired my electricity. One of them still maintains all my power lines. That is how I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you prepared food for them. So what did it look like? What kind of meals? Where did they have their meals? How? Tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Because there was very little food, rather, we had only one kind of food that we all partook of, my wife and I and soldiers and they, and Mr. Martinovic's orders, except that they did not eat in that part of my restaurant where the troops ate, because the entrance to the civilian -- the civilians were not admitted there. So that I took this food to my house, which is right next to the garden, and there is only some flowers in between, and I put up a table for them there and that is where they had their meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: But what else did they do when they were in the base with the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Only those who had some crafts came to work in the unit, that is, people who knew to work about cars, whether it be metalworkers or carpenters or plumbers, car painters, and those who had a craft of some kind. They were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What you personally saw, when you knew of your own knowledge since you saw them often, can you tell us something about the conditions that they worked there under? How were they treated? Were they mistreated? Were they under constant watch? Were they -- did they have any weapons aimed at them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Nobody brought them to our restaurant. They came on their own. At times they would come all together. At times they would come in two or three shifts if they were doing something. I never saw them escorted by guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you see any one of them with bruises or wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: No. Such a person never came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of anyone being killed, any one of those men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know if they stayed overnight in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Some of them, yes, those who had some work to do. When they were not necessary there, then they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know if they received any visits or if they went home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Well, since they were -- since most of them lived near the base, that is Panjevina, in that area there, they allowed to go and visit, I mean those who had their homes there and their families, their wives and children, they were allowed to go there and take them some food, some tinned food or something else, because we had plenty of tins. If their wife was there they could go home and spend the night there and come back the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What did you see? How did Vinko Martinovic treat them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Well, in my view, he treated them correctly. He wasn't too soft on them, but there was no beating or anything, and everybody did what he was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What did you see? How -- what was the treatment and other of his -- how his soldiers treated them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: There was an explicit order, the order from Mr. Martinovic, that without him, nobody could even order a prisoner to go and do something personally. Whatever orders they received, they received them from the commander. Or if a soldier needed something, say his car to be repaired, he had to go to Mr. Martinovic and seek his authorisation to have this done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any of them, that is those prisoners, were in the base, were taken to the front line? You said it was next to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Only in those cases when the vehicle, and the vehicles were very old and broke down very frequently, or if something had to be taken at night-time, dry pack was taken there or a vehicle was stuck there, then a mechanic would take his tools and escorted by a soldier, he's go there to repair it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if during that time that we are talking about, after May, after the 9th of May, 1993, was there any shelling of the town of that area where your restaurant was and where Vinko Martinovic's base was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Yes. I think the base was hit twice. And there were wounded Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French English transcripts among the soldiers, and that whole area, there were quite a number of dead in those buildings nearby. I think it was on the 8th, the 9th. On the same day there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: No. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you -- were you ever at that section of the front line near the health centre on the Bulevar during the conflict between the Army of BH and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: No, never. I -- I'm not a particularly brave person, so I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were you ever in the building housing Vinko Martinovic's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Yes, I was there. I went there often. I told you I went there so that we could see how many meals we had to prepare the next day so that no food would be thrown away, because there were shortages. And that was the only -- the only reason why I went there, to discuss it, how many meals, whether there were any problems about this and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Vinko Martinovic and his unit -- and his soldiers ever drove Muslims out of their homes and looted those flats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: I've heard all kinds of stories, but I cannot personally say. I did not see that, and I think, nevertheless, that it was done by some other units, which were more numerous and which had more men, more vehicles, more trucks, because if 20 soldiers go to the front line and 20 are waiting for it, who is then left to drive people out?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal experience? Did you hear anyone complain that Stela had plundered his property, robbed somebody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: With all those stories that I heard, with all this grapevine, with all these rumours, yes, I've had this experience, and I think it happened in -- I think it was wintertime. So it must have been the winter of 1993, somewhere around the new year. Perhaps after or perhaps before the new year, but at any rate, it was winter time. So everything was happening inside, not in the garden. And a woman in tears came. She could have been 60-ish, 70-ish, and she saw soldiers sitting there. And she cried and asked if anyone could help her because Stela, under the threat of weapons, a pistol, had taken the last hundred marks that she had. And I said to that woman, "Madam, Stela is sitting here. He's been sitting here for the past hour with the town commanders. So he couldn't have done it." "Yes," he said. "Money or I'll kill you." So I went to the next table and I asked him to stand up. "Madam, this is Stela." "No, this is not him. He wears a ponytail and is dark haired." And then Stela took out an identity card with his photograph, and then she started to say, "Who could have been that. Who could have done that?" She was completely aghast. And Mr. Martinovic took out a hundred marks and said, "If somebody took a hundred marks in my name, here, madam, you have a hundred marks, and now you know who Stela is." According to what you saw and heard, how -- what was Vinko Martinovic's attitude toward Muslims? Did he help any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: As to the attitude outside, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: [redacted] And anyway, there were four families that lived next to the base. From the very first moment they were told not to move around. They were at home and that was that. And also in my restaurant before the war and to this day I have a waiter. I've had a waiter, a Muslim. He worked there during the war, and nobody ever mistreated him or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Muslims or, rather, members of their families ever came to the base to ask Vinko Martinovic to help them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that. Not in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we go into private session, please, for several questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you know an individual called Halil Ajanic, nicknamed Lopata?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: I think that every man of common sense understands by the nickname what can be that man. That man is in Mostar known as a bum who has fathered about ten children, but I think he doesn't know how many children he's got. He lives today here, tomorrow somewhere else. He borrows the money from everybody, then he escaped to the other side because he's borrowing this money, and now he hates everything that begins with a "C". About a month ago, he went to a lawyer in front of the municipal court, a lawyer who is a Muslim, Himzo Gakovic. He went to him and broke his windscreens with a stone, only because that lawyer lives on the right bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have completed my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examination. Well, before you start, Mr. Scott, I think right after this afternoon's sitting, one of the Judges has an important meeting to attend, so we'll finish this afternoon's sitting about ten minutes before 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's -- thank you, Your Honour. I think -- I don't think I'll finish in that time but I'll certainly watch the clock and try to stop promptly at ten to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good evening, sir. You were not -- is it correct, sir, from what you've said, I would understand that you were not a member of the HVO military during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The Civil Defence wasn't under the HVO. The Civil Defence was under the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was there any particular reason, sir, that you were not in the HVO military during 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: No. No particular reason. I just said I am not a particularly brave man, so I didn't put on the uniform. And we are two brothers. One of my brothers was in the area of responsibility, so we didn't want both brothers to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So I take there's no effort as to what people refer to as a draft. There was no pressure on you or any sort of draft that would require you to join the army during this time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Listen, had I -- had I not -- had it not been for me, it would have been somebody else who would have to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm not sure I understand that answer, but let me repeat my question. Is it correct, sir, then, that you were free, as you've told us, to stay out of the army, and there was no -- there was no such a thing as a draft or pressure on you to join the HVO military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Nobody forced me to do anything, and I did report at the time of the call-up. I did report, but -- and it fell to my lot to do what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges approximately --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution, Mr. President, since it may tend to identify the witness, could we go to private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I believe you said you saw Stela sometime on the morning of the 9th of May with approximately ten other men. Can you tell us approximately what time of the day on the 9th of May you saw Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Well, early morning hours. I don't know. It was summer, so it could have been 5.00, perhaps half past, perhaps 6.00. I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where was it that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: I saw them as they ran by my restaurant. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French English transcripts

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: And my shop, because my shop is right down the street, and they ran past.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And is that the only time that you saw Stela on the 9th of May, just as he was running by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: No, not the only time, because when they returned, when they were replaced by the next shift, then they came to my terrace, some seven or eight of them out of ten or 11. I told you, I didn't know how many of them. So some eight -- seven or eight of them dropped by and had a drink or something, I suppose. And that is when I knew and how I knew everything that was going on and -- that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so when you say at the end of the shift or before the next shift, approximately how long was it, please, that -- between the time that you saw Stela and his men running by and when they then, some of them, came back to your business later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Since at that time one couldn't have any organised shifts, as it was all spontaneous and people were running from all sides, I can't really tell you. But it could have been around 4.00, maybe 5.00, because at that time there were no organised shifts or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can I understand or more importantly can the Judges understand that between the time you saw Stela running by your restaurant and approximately 4.00 or 5.00 that afternoon you did not see or have any interaction with Stela on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. I didn't because I didn't go to the front line because it's really very near. From the building of the secondary school or from the park one could get hit. And besides, the civilians were not allowed to move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just for clarification's sake, it may have been just interpretation or just a different use of a word, at one point I heard you say that your wife was a member of "the unit." Did you mean to say that she was a member of an HVO unit or did you mean to say she was a member of the restaurant staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: She was a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And which unit was she a member of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Which unit? The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, but which unit within the HVO? Was she a member of Stela's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: I don't know. What she had here was the HVO. Now, what unit or what it was called, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, was she a member of Stela's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what were --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Quartermaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Quartermaster. And what kind of duties -- perhaps some of us can have some idea, but not to speculate, but what her duties as quartermaster of Vinko Martinovic's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: She took over the produce that was brought from the warehouse, prepared the food and then washed the dishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As other HVO soldiers or members of these units, did she receive any sort of compensation or salary as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What were the arrangements, please, by which she would be paid? How did that -- just physically, mechanically, how was payment made to her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: Well, how do I know how? But there will be the list. She'll go there, get the money, sign, just as I did, because in the Civil Defence I also received certain remuneration. Remuneration, you get the money, you sign that you received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me stay with you just for a moment so we can understand it. Is it your understanding, for example, that she would go to Stela's headquarters, from time to time, and receive money for which she would then sign some sort of a record indicating that she had been paid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: I think so. I didn't sign in her name. I didn't go. I didn't accompany her, you know. I don't keep her under my control, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Approximately how many occasions, if you can remember, sir, would she be made? Was she paid once a month, twice a month, or just tell us what you can, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML
utterances.text: I don't really remember. I know it wasn't regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we go back to private session for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go back to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
